key_insight: In strongly stratified flows with no initial vertical shear, horizontal shear instabilities can still generate vertical shear and trigger small-scale diapycnal mixing through two distinct turbulence pathways.
engineering_relevance: This matters for predicting and controlling mixing in geophysical and engineering stratified flows, because horizontal shear alone can produce significant transport when the buoyancy Reynolds number is high enough.
method: Combined linear stability theory with direct numerical simulations.
Compared two routes to turbulence: a vertically-modulated eigenmode pathway and a vertically-invariant columnar-vortex pathway.
Tracked how secondary and tertiary instabilities convert large-scale horizontal shear into buoyancy-scale Kelvin-Helmholtz mixing.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports theory-plus-DNS evidence that the two pathways operate in low-Froude, high-Reynolds-number flows and produce different peak mixing efficiencies.
watch_item: The mixing outcome depends on which instability pathway dominates and on the accessible vertical scales, so predictions may be sensitive to resolution and stratification regime.
paper_title: Two pathways to diapycnal mixing in strongly stratified flows with no initial vertical shear
